toc.title: Slow to bring in the body
When you're not grounded in session

blocks.p: This one is for my fellow therapists, to think about therapy differently, though if you're not a therapist, you're more than welcome to read along. I think transparency is a really good idea when it comes to the process of therapy.
One listener, a therapist, wrote to me:

q: I'm only seven episodes in. I am a CBT and ACT therapist and struggle myself. There is something missing from these therapies: the body. I am so interested in Polyvagal Theory, and I'm hoping it will really help me and my clients. Since listening to your podcast, I have been reflecting on how I am not often in a safe and social state during sessions. I'm a bit hyped up and worried about not being helpful. I have been trying to do belly breathing before and during sessions. Anything else you would recommend? I think I've found the missing piece!!!!!

blocks.p: I absolutely agree about the missing piece. Her message spurred me to go in a different direction first, so I'll start there, and then I'll answer her question more directly.

Psychology has dominated the world of thought: cognitions, cognitive and psychological theory, relationships, behavior. That has been our domain for quite a while. It's been our specialty, and it's how we've been relevant to the world, how we've contributed, hopefully, to making the world a better place. Thought, relationships, behavior, and we do it through our theoretical constructs.

So we have owned the world of mental health, and a lot of the time we've thought about mental health as a thinking problem, some sort of cognitive deficit, or maybe a behavioral problem. The theories and the process of therapy change, yes. But when it comes down to it, I don't think we've contributed anything brand new in quite a while. We've traditionally looked at change as a thought problem or a behavioral problem.

At the time of this episode, it seemed like mental health had taken quite a hit, especially during the pandemic. I hadn't looked at stats, so this was just me looking in from the outside. But there's a lot of need out there, and a higher awareness of mental health issues. People encourage others to seek help. So you'd think therapy has become more relevant.

There's a big need for services to help people change, but not for therapy. That might seem to contradict itself, but it doesn't. There's a need for support, yes. There's a need for mental health help, absolutely. There's a need for people to make change in their lives, 100%. So you'd think, "Therefore, therapy." But no. They need change. They don't necessarily need therapy.

And all of this is happening along with the internet, which has drastically changed everything. The internet has made it very easy for other people to say, "Hey, I can help in my own way." There are plenty of people doing something similar to therapy who don't call themselves therapists. They provide a similar service, and they're willing to go beyond cognitions and behavior and incorporate whatever they can to establish their own thing.

You've probably heard of coaches of all kinds: relationship coaches, business coaches, coaches who specialize in trauma. They're willing to do cognitions. They're willing to look at the body. They're willing to look at psychological theory. They'll incorporate whatever they can in order to make an impact in people's lives.

They don't need our theories. They don't need to look at things as a psychological construct, as if there are parts within us communicating with each other, like a protective part and a child part. Psychology has generally claimed those things: "This is how we view a human being, and this is how change happens." Coaches and other helpers can do that too, but they can also incorporate somatic pieces of change, gut health, generational trauma, personal responsibility. They can highlight any of these areas, and they don't have to worry about all the psychological theory that we, in my opinion, spend way too much time on.

Even the approaches the listener mentioned, ACT and CBT, already have coaching versions. You don't have to be a therapist to implement ACT. CBT has coaching aspects already. Internal Family Systems, with its child parts and protective parts, has its own coaching apparatus as well.

So in my opinion, our relevance dwindles, because we've been so focused on theoretical constructs, on thinking as the problem or behavior as the problem, and really slow to incorporate the somatic pieces.

blocks.h: Slow to bring in the body

blocks.p: Take Somatic Experiencing from Peter Levine. I wouldn't call that coaching. It's a modality that focuses on trauma in particular, but you don't have to be a therapist for it. You could just be a person who says, "I've taken this training, I've gotten a certain level of proficiency in it, and I'm offering my service."

I'm not knocking coaches, and I'm not knocking SE practitioners whatsoever. What I'm probably more knocking is therapists, for being really slow, like the listener says, to bring in other pieces that could be helpful. Somatic Experiencing has been around for decades. It's not new. The somatic information, and how it can be relevant to therapy, has been out there.

I didn't get that in therapy school. I graduated around 2008, and it was not an aspect of my schooling at all. I had to learn it after school. I've heard from some students who follow my work that they're getting more and more of it now, and that's great. But this information has been out there, and therapy has absolutely lagged when it comes to the somatic pieces of change.

So now we're in a position where we're no longer special. Therapists had a pretty special role. People who needed change needed to go to someone, a change agent, we'll call them. But change, and being a change agent, is not exclusively ours anymore. And when it comes to the somatic pieces of change, we definitely do not own that.

Because when it comes down to it, it's really just some basic biological stuff, and then accessing it through mindfulness: being able to attach your conscious self to your somatic self, as if they were two different things. They're not, but conceptually I'll put it that way.

So there's a very low entry point. Anybody can do this, and I think that's been part of psychology's reluctance to implement it more: it's not special to us. There are no diagnoses to worry about, no complexes, no theoretical constructs you really need. And there are no prescribed norms of behavior. I think psychology has stumbled there, saying, "We know what is the norm of behavior, and we know what is not." When it comes to the somatic pieces of who we are, I wouldn't say there's normal or abnormal. It's more about what is ideal for survival.

When we talk about biology, it's really evolution and survival. What evolved within us that was ideal for surviving in those conditions, and how does it affect us now? It's not about being the arbiters of what is normal and what is disordered. That's not necessary. So our relevance in dictating what's normal and not normal isn't really there anymore.

I can see why psychology has been reluctant to adopt the somatic pieces of change. It's not about diagnosis. We don't get to hide behind our diagnoses anymore and say, "We know more than you, and here you go." We are not the experts on your life. We are not the experts on your biology. And that makes us less special.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: Psychology has looked at thought and behavior. When we look at the Polyvagal Theory and the somatic aspects of who we are, we know that thought and behavior follow the somatic aspects. They influence each other too. But story follows state: our cognitions follow the state our body is in, our autonomic nervous system. Behavior does as well. Our behavior is largely dictated by the state we're in and the types of behavior it gives us access to. We don't do prosocial behaviors unless we're in our safety state.

So I don't think what we've focused on over the years has been wrong, but it's obviously missing a huge, huge piece. And now that we have a deeper understanding of that piece, in my opinion the priority is the somatic aspects, and then how they fit into our larger consciousness: our behaviors, our thoughts, our cognitions. Rather than cognitions and behavior being the priority, it's mindfully being with the somatic aspects, self-regulating on a nervous system level, and then behaviors and thoughts change.

In my opinion, if you're a therapist and you don't understand these very basic aspects of what it means to be human, to be mammals, and what it means for us to make change, you're way behind, and you're doing a disservice to your clients.

That's me going off a little. It's pretty upsetting to see the state of a profession I love so much. Hopefully we incorporate these things faster and continue to stay relevant. People need change. They don't need therapists. Therapists can be an aspect of change, and I hope we can step up more. But people will find change elsewhere.

blocks.h: When you're not grounded in session

blocks.p: Now to the listener's question, about grounding in session.

First, I want to normalize and validate this. It's normal for us therapists to feel anxiety, or whatever it is, during our sessions. We want to help. We want to be effective change agents. We want to be relevant in our clients' lives, provide a good service, and help people meet their goals. So we're excited about our role. We have energy for this, hopefully. But at the same time, we might be insecure about our own competency, and maybe not just our competency, but who we are as people. We might not have the highest self-esteem. We're human.
So I want to reframe this. Rather than "I'm not good enough" or "I'm incompetent at my job," let's reframe it as "I'm excited to help."

Let's look at excitement a little deeper. Being excited, in my understanding, requires that we have access to our safety state. We have that flight and fight energy, we're mobilized, but we need access to our safety state for that mobilized energy to feel like excitement.

If the safety state is turned off, if the vagal brake comes off, then it's just flight and fight energy, and it turns into anxiety, or aggression, or something else. If your safe and social state isn't active, you drop down the ladder into sympathetic arousal. It'll probably feel like nervousness or worry. You might be more fidgety. It might feel like anxiety.

And when we as therapists get more dysregulated, especially in a mobilized way, we tend to have an impulse to fill up any silence in the session. That's not about the client. That's about us. And if there's silence and it isn't filled, story follows state. We're already feeling anxious, and during that silence we tell ourselves, "Oh my God, I'm failing. The client knows I'm not doing a good job. They're going to walk out on me, I'm going to lose a client, and now I can't pay the rent." All of that goes through a therapist's mind.

The thoughts in our mind follow the state we're in. If you're in a very anxious flight state, your thoughts will be more fearful and more anxious, and that feeds back into your somatic self and keeps it going. It's a loop.

Deep breathing, like the listener said, can be great to slow your system down. When you inhale, your heart rate kicks up a little. The exhale is where it actually slows down and the parasympathetic, the safety state, comes on. So when you do some deep breathing, slow your breath on the way out. That can really help your whole body slow down. And do it mindfully. Really notice what it feels like to extend your exhale and for your body to settle and slow.

Beyond that, what works for you as an individual? I'm very reluctant to say, "Just do this and you're good." You need to be able to listen to what your body needs, and that's something to practice outside of session: identifying what brings you to safety or not. Then, before a session, you'll know what state you're in, or at least feel what kind of energy you have, and you'll know, "This technique helps me climb my [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) when I'm in this state."
You might want to stretch out. You might want to push. You might want to do a jiggle, a bop, a sway.

For me, I've done deep breathing before and during sessions. Stretching before a session helps me sometimes. Before a live stream or an interview where I'm being interviewed, there have been times I've done pushups. Not to make myself look bigger before the interview, but because I have that tension inside me. My muscles are tense, or my breathing is shallow, so I do something physical to help relieve it, and that helps me a lot. Stretching on the carpet has helped me a lot too.

Back then, I did therapy one-on-one with adults at night, and in the daytime I did therapy with high schoolers. At the high school, I wasn't going to be stretching out on the floor before a session. What helped there was a deep breath beforehand, and just telling myself, "Let's go." That cognitive, top-down approach.

I was often more wound up there, and that's very normal working at a high school. That year there were a lot of crises, a lot of panicky flavor in the students I worked with, a lot of mental health concerns, and a lot of grief we were dealing with. So I already had amped energy pretty often, and I didn't necessarily want to slow it down. I'd tell myself, "Let's go. Let's use this energy for good," and that helped me point it in the right direction.
Having more energy before a session is not a bad thing. It's about whether you can contain it, feel it, and use it appropriately. If you lose access to your safety state, then it becomes a problem.

So for me, that top-down attitude helped: "Let's go," or "I got this," or "F it, I'm jumping into this crisis situation. I'll do the best I can." In a job with crises, not just someone showing up to session in a bad mood, but someone suicidal, or a fight that might be breaking out, someone says, "Hey, we need your help," and you're on your way. You don't have time to stretch out and do deep breathing. You say, "Okay, let's do it," and you do the best you can with that mindset. That works for me.

If I feel that energy ramping up, a lot of the time just changing my position helps. Leaning forward, especially if the client is leaning forward, kind of mirroring them, can be really helpful. Sometimes just switching my position helps somehow. I don't even know how, but switching it up gets me out of that somatic defensive energy in the moment.

You can also clench your muscles and relax them while you're sitting in your therapy chair. Tense and relax your calves, your forearms, whatever it is, subtly. Maybe they're picking up on it neuroceptively, but consciously no one is going to know you're doing it.

Identifying what brings you to safety ahead of time can also help you set up your therapy room with more of a feeling of safety. We never really know what our clients will feel safe with, though there are some general things. But at least for you, you can build in elements of safety.

One more thing about these defensive feelings in session. They might not be a bad thing. They might actually be a really good thing, because what you're feeling might be empathy. It might not be your own stuff. It could be. But it could also be a clue to what the client across from you is going through, and that can be a really helpful tool for therapy.

That happens to me a lot. If I have a slight sensation of disconnection, that's a clue my client may be going through something similar. So we have to be able to discern: is that my stuff, or their stuff? If you have empathy, you can feel what they're feeling. If you have compassion, you can feel what they're feeling and still have access to your safety state.

Oftentimes in session, I'll have tightness in some muscles, tension, shallow breath, maybe even a flavor of panic, or a disconnection. I gauge whether it's my stuff or theirs, and I use it as a prompt to check in with the client about how they're doing in that moment. I'm consistently surprised at how accurate this can be.

I don't typically say, "Hey, here are my feelings. Are you feeling them too?" If you can own that and use it responsibly in session, I don't think there's anything wrong with it. That's just not how I typically work. I'll say, "Hey, what's going on for you right now? How are you feeling right now?" Then I bring their attention inward and get more specific. I won't say, "My breathing is shallow. How about you?" I'll say, "Check in with your breathing. How's your breathing right now?" Or, "How's your muscle tension?" Or, "Do a body scan. How are you feeling right now?"

These somatic clues, as I call them, can be super helpful in session. It's not necessarily because you're dysregulated. It might be a reflection of what the client is going through. That's fantastic. You just have to be able to discern. And if it is your own sensation, you have to figure out what grounds you. I can't tell anybody else that.
